evidence_quotes.quote: De acuerdo al último censo nacional (2010), en el área metropolitana, el 86,2 % de los hogares tienen servicios de agua potable y solo el 63,5 % de los hogares posee servicios de desagüe cloacal.
In order to address this issue we analyze institutional changes in the company providing water and sewerage services from the early twentieth century to the present.

Al mantener, en términos generales, el régimen tarifario de OSN, la incorporación de nuevos usuarios predominantemente pobres y localizados en zonas de difícil acceso se transformó en irrelevante en términos de la rentabilidad de la empresa concesionaria, una situación que se tornaba todavía más crítica cuando era necesario invertir en la construcción de grandes obras de potabilización o de depuración de efluentes.

A diferencia del esquema anterior, en el que las obras e inversiones se acordaban entre la empresa concesionaria y los funcionarios nacionales, el nuevo marco regulatorio estableció que los planes de expansión del servicio fueran definidos por la mencionada agencia de planificación con la participación de la Nación, los municipios, la ciudad de Buenos Aires y AySA.

En la segunda parte, se analizan tres momentos de la gestión del agua que dejaron huellas en el territorio metropolitano. Finalmente, las conclusiones intentan inscribir el análisis de los cambios institucionales en una comprensión más general, sobre cómo se construye y politiza el territorio metropolitano en los intersticios de las políticas sectoriales y centralizadas.
Para comprender y explicar este fenómeno se propone la reconstrucción de los cambios institucionales y de la historia urbana de las redes técnicas.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and metropolitan access to piped drinking water and sewerage network services (servicios de agua y desagüe cloacal) across the Buenos Aires Metropolitan Area.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording: Yes — examines institutional, ownership, regulatory, and governance changes across three eras of water/sewerage management (Obras Sanitarias de la Nación 1912-1993, private concession Aguas Argentinas S.A. and regulator ETOSS 1993-2006, and re-nationalized Agua y Saneamientos Argentinos S.A. with APLA and ERAS from 2006). Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Yes (borderline) — although framed broadly around macro-historical territorialization, the paper specifically discusses rule-type mechanisms directly governing service expansion and access, including utility ownership and regulatory structure (state monopoly vs. canon-free private concession with contractual universal coverage mandates vs. state enterprise with municipal planning via APLA) and tariff/cost-recovery rules (uniform unmetered 'canilla libre' tariff removing profitability incentives for Aguas Argentinas to connect low-income peripheral households). Both readings yield overall exclusion because the paper lacks empirical evidence (Criterion 3).
criterion_notes.c3: No — this is a historical-institutional narrative overview and conceptual essay reconstructing utility history from secondary literature, with no empirical research design, no methods section, no primary qualitative or quantitative data collection, and no systematic empirical synthesis (exclude as E05). The only statistics in the article are a single cross-sectional 2010 Census background snapshot of metropolitan water/sewerage coverage (p. 4) and a national 1895-2010 urban/rural population table (Table 1, p. 6).
criterion_notes.c4: Unclear — cites descriptive 2010 Census household connection rates for piped water (86.2% overall; 97% in Buenos Aires City vs. 72.1% in surrounding municipalities) and sewerage (63.5% overall; 98% vs. 40.5%) as setting background and makes qualitative historical assertions about connected central vs. disconnected peripheral areas, but reports no empirical access outcomes evaluated for or across the three institutional regimes.
criterion_notes.c5: No — while the geographic setting (Buenos Aires Metropolitan Area) and historical institutional shifts are described, there is no identifiable empirical study design, no empirical sample or unit-of-analysis data strategy, and no empirically measured outcome linked to the institutional exposures.
criterion_notes.c6: Yes (via Criterion 10) — main text is in Spanish (with bilingual Spanish/English title and abstract), rather than English, Portuguese, or Dutch (Criterion 9), but full text is completely readable and translation is directly feasible; assessed directly from the Spanish text.

population_and_sample: Buenos Aires Metropolitan Area (Ciudad Autónoma de Buenos Aires and 24 surrounding municipalities of Buenos Aires Province; 12,806,866 inhabitants in 2010 Census); no empirical study sample
exposure: Institutional, utility-ownership, regulatory, and tariff models across three historical stages: centralized state enterprise Obras Sanitarias de la Nación (1912-1993) with uniform unmetered tariffs, private concession Aguas Argentinas S.A. with tripartite regulator ETOSS (1993-2006), and re-nationalized Agua y Saneamientos Argentinos S.A. with planning agency APLA and regulator ERAS (2006-present)
outcome: Narrative historical discussion of spatial inequality and territorialization of water and sewerage network coverage (with descriptive 2010 Census household connection rates cited only as background context, and no empirical outcome measurement across regimes)
rationale: Full-text Spanish article matching record metadata (Catenazzi 2017, DOI 10.17561/at.10.3612). Although the paper discusses water and sewerage network access in Metropolitan Buenos Aires (c1=yes) and traces institutional, ownership, regulatory, and tariff structures across OSN, Aguas Argentinas, and AySA (c2=yes under plain wording and borderline yes under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading via utility ownership/regulatory structure and tariff rules), it is a non-empirical historical-institutional narrative essay based on secondary literature with no empirical research design, no methods or primary data, and no empirical evaluation of access outcomes across the three utility periods (only a descriptive 2010 Census background snapshot on p. 4 and a national urbanization table on p. 6). Excluded under E05 (No empirical evidence) under both narrow and plain readings of Criterion 2.
